concept.name: Central counterparty
concept.definition: A central counterparty (CCP) is a clearing organization that interposes itself between the parties to a trade, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, thereby guaranteeing performance and mutualizing counterparty credit risk. In U.S. futures markets a CCP registered with the CFTC is known as a derivatives clearing organization (DCO).
concept.intuition: A CCP is the market's middleman-of-last-resort: after your trade is done, you no longer rely on the stranger you traded with — you rely on the clearing house, which stands behind every trade.
concept.mechanics: Through novation, the CCP replaces the original bilateral contract with two contracts against itself. It collects initial and variation margin from clearing members daily, maintains a default fund and other resources, and runs default-management ('waterfall') procedures to absorb a member's failure while continuing to perform on all other trades.
concept.failure_modes: CCPs concentrate risk: a default exceeding margin plus the default fund can force loss mutualization onto surviving members or, in extremis, CCP failure. Procyclical margin increases in stress can drain market-wide liquidity, and CCP risk models can be wrong about tail correlations.
concept.misconceptions: Central clearing does not eliminate counterparty risk — it transforms and concentrates it in the CCP with a layered default waterfall. Nor is every cleared product equally safe: clearing guarantees performance, not price outcomes.
concept.example: Two firms trade an interest-rate swap cleared at a CCP; when one member later defaults, the CCP uses the defaulter's margin and default-fund contributions to honor the swap, and the surviving counterparty is unaffected.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
